source.title: On the importance of initialization and momentum in deep learning
source.venue: Proceedings of the 30th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 28(3), 1139–1147

digest.question: Why does momentum speed up gradient descent, and when does it get in the way?

hookResult.text: Momentum lets descent build up speed in directions that keep reducing the loss, and training does markedly worse when it is absent or poorly tuned.

counterfactual.expectedQualitativeEffect: With no momentum the ball creeps along the valley's floor: at step 36 it is more than 0.5 further from the lowest point.

difference.label: Distance from the lowest point at step 36

beginner.text: The ball rolls downhill one step at a time. Each step, the slope under it says which way is down. With momentum, the ball also keeps some of the speed it already had, so along a long gentle valley its speed builds up, and it gets to the bottom sooner.
beginner.analogy: Like a sledge on a long, gentle hill: it starts slowly, but it keeps its speed from one moment to the next and soon runs fast.

intermediate.text: Each step adds the slope's push to a velocity, and the velocity moves the ball. Momentum sets how much of the last velocity is kept: at 0 each step starts afresh, at 0.9 most of it carries over. Along the valley's floor the slope keeps pointing the same way, so the velocity grows, step after step.

advanced.text: Classical momentum keeps a velocity v: each step decays it by μ and adds −ε times the gradient, then moves θ by v. At λ = 0 the gradient is taken where the ball stands. In a direction where the gradient keeps its sign, v grows towards ε·|∇f|/(1 − μ), ten times a plain step at μ = 0.9.
advanced.equation: v ← μ·v − ε·∇f(θ + λ·μ·v),  θ ← θ + v

counterfactual.prompt: What if the momentum were halved, to 0.5?
counterfactual.expectedQualitativeEffect: With half the momentum less speed carries over: the longest step within 60 steps is more than 0.1 shorter.

beginner.text: This time the ball starts low on the valley's side, so it mostly rolls along the floor. Each step is pushed by the slope and carries on with the speed it had, so the steps grow longer and longer until the ball nears the bottom.
beginner.analogy: Like pushing a child on a swing: small pushes, each in time with the last, add up to a big swing.

intermediate.text: Along the valley's floor the slope keeps pointing the same way. Each step adds the same small push to a velocity that keeps most of itself, so the steps lengthen. The step size scales every push; momentum sets how much of the velocity survives from one step to the next.

advanced.text: On a constant slope c, v_k = −ε·c·(1 − μ^k)/(1 − μ): the steps grow towards ε·c/(1 − μ). At μ = 0.5 that limit is twice a plain step; at μ = 0.9, ten times. Directions of low curvature change their gradient slowly, so momentum amplifies them.

counterfactual.prompt: What if it took the gradient a step ahead, as Nesterov's method does?
counterfactual.expectedQualitativeEffect: Looking ahead, the ball stops swinging from wall to wall: its path within 96 steps is more than 2 shorter.

beginner.text: Across the valley the walls are steep. With a lot of momentum the ball overshoots the floor, climbs the other wall, and swings back, again and again, before it settles. Nesterov's method looks a little ahead before it pushes, and catches the swing early.
beginner.analogy: Like steering a bicycle: if you correct only where you are, you weave; if you look a little ahead, you ride straight.

intermediate.text: Classical momentum takes the gradient where the ball stands. Nesterov's accelerated gradient first moves the ball by its momentum, μ·v, and takes the gradient there. On a steep wall that gradient already points back, so the velocity is corrected before the overshoot, not after.

advanced.text: With λ = 1 the gradient is taken at θ + μ·v. On a direction of curvature h this multiplies the kept velocity by μ·(1 − ε·h) rather than μ, a smaller effective momentum where the curvature is high, which damps the oscillation.
advanced.equation: v ← μ·v − ε·∇f(θ + λ·μ·v),  θ ← θ + v

counterfactual.prompt: What if the momentum were turned up to 0.99?
counterfactual.expectedQualitativeEffect: With nearly all its speed kept, the ball keeps overshooting: at step 150 it is more than 0.5 further from the lowest point.

difference.label: Distance from the lowest point at step 150

beginner.text: Momentum helps the ball get going, but it also keeps the ball going. With too much, the ball rolls past the bottom, up the other side and back, and takes a long time to settle.
beginner.analogy: Like a heavy cart on a dip in the road: it does not stop at the bottom, it rolls back and forth for a long time.

intermediate.text: Each step keeps a share μ of the velocity. At 0.8 a swing dies away in a few dozen steps; at 0.99 it keeps almost all of itself, so the ball overshoots the bottom and swings for hundreds of steps before it settles.

advanced.text: When the swing is underdamped, each step shrinks it by about √μ: 0.89 at μ = 0.8, but 0.995 at μ = 0.99. After 150 steps that leaves under a millionth of the swing at μ = 0.8, and nearly half at μ = 0.99.

counterfactual.prompt: What if momentum 0.9 were added to this big step?
counterfactual.expectedQualitativeEffect: Added to a step already big for the steep walls, momentum sets the ball swinging: over 60 steps the loss is higher by more than 0.5 on average.

difference.label: The loss on average over 60 steps

beginner.text: Momentum is not free. With big steps, plain gradient descent already comes down the steep walls quickly. Adding a lot of momentum on top makes the ball overshoot and swing, so it does worse, not better.
beginner.analogy: Like pushing a swing harder while it is already high: the push and the swing together carry it too far.

intermediate.text: The best momentum depends on the step size and on how curved the valley is. A step size that suits plain descent on the steep walls, with 0.9 of the velocity kept, overshoots each wall and rings, and the loss stays high for longer.

advanced.text: Across the valley, ε·h = 0.06 × 25 = 1.5: plain descent shrinks the swing by |1 − 1.5| = 0.5 a step. With μ = 0.9 the roots of λ² − (1 + μ − ε·h)·λ + μ = 0 are complex, of modulus √0.9 ≈ 0.95, so the swing dies away far more slowly.

limits.text: A miniature: two dimensions stand in for the millions a deep network's loss has. The paper's experiments, deep autoencoders and recurrent networks trained for many hours, are not reproduced, and none of its results is.
The valley, its curvatures, the step sizes, the momenta and the ball's starting points are teaching choices, not the paper's.
The paper raises the momentum slowly during training, by a schedule; here each run keeps one momentum throughout.

The surface has no noise and the rule no chance, so the same settings always give the same run. Each level's statement is checked on the world's own settings and starting point and on 19 others, each within a tenth of them, not on 20 seeds.
